Canadian visa and immigration basics

Plain-language guide · reviewed for general accuracy · Canada, 2026

Canada's immigration system can feel overwhelming, with many programs, pathways, and acronyms. This guide gives you a high-level picture of the main options — whether you're looking to visit, study, work, or settle permanently. Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) is the federal department that handles most applications.

1. Visiting Canada: visas and eTAs

If you're visiting for tourism, business meetings, or to see family (usually up to six months), you may need a visitor visa (temporary resident visa, or TRV) or an Electronic Travel Authorization (eTA). Citizens of visa-exempt countries (including the US, UK, Australia, and most EU members) only need an eTA, which costs CAD $7 and is linked electronically to your passport. Others must apply for a visitor visa, which requires showing ties to your home country, sufficient funds, and a clear purpose for your visit. A visitor visa does not allow you to work.

2. Studying in Canada: study permits

To study at a designated learning institution (DLI) in Canada for more than six months, you generally need a study permit. You must first be accepted by a DLI, then apply for the permit. A study permit typically allows you to work up to 20 hours per week off-campus during academic sessions and full-time during scheduled breaks. After graduation, many international students become eligible for a Post-Graduation Work Permit (PGWP), which can be a stepping stone to permanent residence through Express Entry.

3. Working in Canada: work permits

Most foreign nationals need a work permit to work in Canada. There are two broad categories: employer-specific (closed) work permits tied to a particular job and employer, and open work permits that allow you to work for almost any employer. Employer-specific permits often require a Labour Market Impact Assessment (LMIA) showing that no Canadian could fill the role. Open work permits are available in specific situations — for spouses of international students or skilled workers, recent graduates, or as bridging permits while a PR application is pending.

4. Permanent residence: the main pathways

The largest economic immigration program is Express Entry, a points-based system that ranks candidates on factors like age, education, work experience, and language ability in English or French. Top-ranked candidates receive an Invitation to Apply (ITA) for permanent residence. Alongside Express Entry, each province (except Quebec) runs its own Provincial Nominee Program (PNP), which can nominate candidates who meet local labour needs. Quebec operates its own immigration system with separate criteria. Family sponsorship lets Canadian citizens and permanent residents sponsor a spouse, common-law partner, dependent child, or (with limitations) parent or grandparent.

Important: only authorized immigration consultants (members of CICC) and lawyers in good standing with a provincial law society can charge a fee to give Canadian immigration advice. Check credentials before paying anyone.

5. Staying in status — don't let it lapse

If your temporary status (visitor, student, or worker) is about to expire, apply to extend it before it does. If you apply before expiry, you generally have "implied status" and can stay under the same conditions until a decision is made. Falling out of status can have serious consequences, including being asked to leave Canada. Restoration of status is possible within 90 days in some cases, but it's better never to need it.

Common questions

What are the main ways to get permanent residence?
Express Entry (points-based for skilled workers), Provincial Nominee Programs, family sponsorship, and Quebec's separate programs.
Do I need a visa to visit Canada?
It depends on your citizenship. Many countries are visa-exempt and only need an eTA (CAD $7). Others need a visitor visa.
Can I work while my PR application is being processed?
Not automatically. You need a valid work permit or a Bridging Open Work Permit if your current permit is expiring and your PR application is in process.
